title: Concepts: what each piece is
description: Clusters, nodes, taints, contexts, kubeconfig, namespaces and Services, explained once so the guides can refer back to them.

html:
Read this once. The guides (Create a local Kubernetes cluster with kind, Create a local Kubernetes cluster with k3d, Deploy apps into your namespaces, one at a time) refer back to these ideas.

#The big picture

You want a real Kubernetes cluster on your own computer to learn on, without cloud bills or risk. kind makes one out of Docker containers:

Inside the nodes, your applications run as pods, grouped into namespaces:

#kind

Kubernetes in Docker. Each Kubernetes node is one Docker container that itself runs Kubernetes components. The result behaves like a real multi-machine cluster: same kubectl, same YAML, same objects. Delete the cluster and nothing else on your Mac is touched. It is for learning and testing, not production.

#Cluster, nodes, control plane

  • Cluster — the whole thing: one control plane plus workers.
  • Control-plane node — runs the API server (what kubectl talks to), the scheduler (decides which node runs each pod), and etcd (the cluster's database). It is tainted so ordinary pods stay off it.
  • Worker node — runs your pods.

kind fixes the node list at creation. To change it, delete the cluster and create it again from an edited config file.

#Names, kubeconfig and contexts

~/.kube/config lists every cluster kubectl knows, and how to log in. A context is one entry: cluster + user (+ optional default namespace). The current context is where every command goes. kind create cluster adds kind-<cluster name> and switches to it; k3d cluster create does the same with k3d-<cluster name>.

Why it matters: if the same file holds a cloud or work cluster, running kubectl delete while the wrong context is current deletes things there. Check with kubectl config current-context.

#Where the name comes from

name: is the cluster's name. kind uses it in two places:

  • the node containers are named <name>-control-plane, <name>-worker, <name>-worker2;
  • the kubectl context is named kind-<name>.

Without that line, kind falls back to the name kind: nodes called kind-control-plane and a context called kind-kind.

The same name can be given on the command line, where it overrides the file:

#The kind- prefix is added by kind

When kind create cluster finishes, it writes new entries into ~/.kube/config, named kind- plus the cluster name. The prefix is fixed; the config file cannot change it. It exists so kind clusters are easy to spot next to cloud ones such as gke_... in kubectl config get-contexts.

To use another context name, rename it afterwards (see "They are separate" below).

#The kubeconfig file: three lists and a pointer

~/.kube/config holds three separate lists, plus the current context:

ThingWhat it isHolds
Cluster (kubeconfig entry)The address of an API serverURL and CA certificate
UserAn identityCertificate and key, or a token
ContextA named pairing of one cluster and one userPointers to the other two, and an optional default namespace

kubectl only ever uses contexts. When you run kubectl get pods, it takes the current context, follows its cluster pointer to find where to send the request, and follows its user pointer to find how to authenticate.

#A fourth name: kind's own

local-cluster-1, without the prefix, is the name kind knows the cluster by:

kind is not kubectl, so it does not use kubeconfig names. It uses the name: from your config file.

All the names side by side:

NameUsed byExample
local-cluster-1kind commands, node container nameskind get nodes --name local-cluster-1
kind-local-cluster-1 (cluster entry)kubeconfig internalsrarely typed
kind-local-cluster-1 (user entry)kubeconfig internalsrarely typed
kind-local-cluster-1 (context)kubectlkubectl config use-context kind-local-cluster-1

#Namespaces

Folders inside a cluster. They separate teams or environments, let two apps use the same name, and let you list or delete one group at a time (-n <name> on commands, -A for all). Deleting a namespace deletes everything in it. They are not a security wall by themselves.

#The system namespaces

Every cluster starts with a few namespaces that Kubernetes creates for itself. Your apps do not go in them. This section says what each one holds, so you recognise what you see and know what is safe to leave alone.

NamespaceOne-line purpose
kube-systemThe cluster's own components: DNS, networking, the control plane
kube-publicInformation that anyone, even without logging in, may read
kube-node-leaseOne small heartbeat object per node
defaultWhere objects go when you give no -n; yours to use

#kube-system

The home of the cluster's own machinery. What is inside depends on the kind of cluster.

#In a kind cluster (the 3-node cluster from Create a local Kubernetes cluster with kind)
PodKindWhat it does
kube-apiserver-<control-plane>static podThe API server: what kubectl talks to
etcd-<control-plane>static podThe cluster's database
kube-scheduler-<control-plane>static podPicks a node for each new pod
kube-controller-manager-<control-plane>static podRuns the loops that keep reality matching your Deployments and the like
coredns-… (usually 2)DeploymentCluster DNS: how web.web becomes an IP
kube-proxy-… (one per node)DaemonSetMakes Services work by routing traffic to their pods
kindnet-… (one per node)DaemonSetThe network plugin: gives pods IPs and lets them reach each other

Terms:

  • Static pod: started by a node's kubelet from a file on disk, not by a Deployment. The name ends with the node name. In kind the files are in /etc/kubernetes/manifests on the control-plane node.
  • DaemonSet: runs one pod on every node. A 3-node cluster has three kube-proxy and three kindnet pods.

Besides pods, the namespace holds:

  • the Service kube-dns (the stable address in front of coredns);
  • ConfigMaps such as coredns and kube-proxy (their settings);
  • ServiceAccounts, and bootstrap tokens used when nodes join;
  • Leases used for leader election between components.

kind's local storage provisioner is not here; it has its own namespace, local-path-storage.

#In k3s and k3d

coredns, local-path-provisioner, metrics-server and traefik (the bundled ingress), plus svclb-… pods for LoadBalancer Services. k3s runs the control plane inside one process, so there are no separate kube-apiserver, etcd or kube-scheduler pods.

#In GKE

Google runs the control plane, so there is no kube-apiserver or etcd pod to see. Typically present: kube-dns and kube-dns-autoscaler, metrics-server, konnectivity-agent, the persistent disk driver (pdcsi-node), logging and metrics agents (fluentbit-…, gke-metrics-agent), and network pods (netd or anetd). The exact list varies with the cluster's settings.

#Rules of thumb
  • Do not deploy your own apps into kube-system.
  • Do not delete things there casually. Deleting coredns breaks DNS for the whole cluster; deleting kube-proxy breaks Services.
  • When pods cannot resolve names or reach Services, kube-system is the first place to look.
#Looking at it

All the components and the node each runs on.

Which are per-node and which are replicated.

The static pod files on the kind control-plane node: etcd.yaml, kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml.

#kube-public

A namespace whose contents can be read by everyone, including users who are not logged in. It is meant for cluster information that must be available before anyone has credentials.

#What is in it

Normally one ConfigMap:

cluster-info holds a small kubeconfig fragment: the API server's address and the cluster's CA certificate. A new node reads it when joining a cluster built with kubeadm, to find the API server and to check it is talking to the right one. kind builds its nodes with kubeadm, so it is there.

#Facts
  • There are no pods in it, and your apps do not go there.
  • The public read access comes from a Role and RoleBinding that grant it to anonymous users. Nothing in this namespace should be secret.
  • Many managed clusters, GKE included, leave kube-public empty or unused.
  • It is rarely touched in day-to-day work. Seeing it empty is normal.

#kube-node-lease

A namespace that holds one Lease object per node. A Lease is a tiny record with a name, an owner and a "last renewed" timestamp.

#What it is for

Each node's kubelet renews its own Lease every few seconds (about 10 by default). That is the node's heartbeat: "I am alive". The control plane watches the timestamps. If a Lease has not been renewed for around 40–50 seconds, the node is marked NotReady (shown as Unknown in some outputs), and pods on it are later rescheduled elsewhere.

Before Leases, each heartbeat updated the whole Node object, which is large; with many nodes that put real load on etcd. A Lease is small and cheap to update, so the heartbeat can be frequent without cost. The full Node status is now updated much less often.

#Looking at it

One Lease per node, named after the node.

The renewTime field changes every few seconds. Run it twice to watch it move.

#Facts
  • There are no pods in it, and nothing for you to manage; it is entirely automatic.
  • The Lease is deleted when its node is removed from the cluster.
  • Components such as the scheduler also use Leases for leader election, but those live in kube-system, not here.
  • Stopping a node container (docker stop local-cluster-1-worker) stops its Lease renewals; after the grace period the node goes NotReady. That is a quick way to watch the mechanism work.

#Side by side

kube-systemkube-publickube-node-lease
HoldsCluster components (pods, Services, ConfigMaps)One ConfigMap, cluster-infoOne Lease per node
Pods insideYesNoNo
Who can readCluster adminsEveryone, anonymous includedCluster admins
Changes over timeWhen components restart or upgradeAlmost neverEvery few seconds, automatic
You shouldLook, don't touchLeave aloneLeave alone

#Taints and tolerations

A label lets a pod choose a node. A taint works the other way round: it is a "keep out" sign on a node. The scheduler will not place a pod on a tainted node unless the pod carries a matching permission slip, a toleration.

A taint is written key=value:effect, for example dedicated=data:NoSchedule.

EffectWhat it does
NoScheduleNew pods without a toleration are not placed here. Pods already running stay.
PreferNoScheduleA soft version: avoided, but used if nothing else fits.
NoExecuteAlso evicts pods already running there that do not tolerate it.

A toleration names the taint it covers (key, effect) and how to compare it (operator):

operatorMatches whenvalue
Existsthe node has a taint with that key, whatever its valueleave it out
Equal (the default)the key and the value are both the samerequired

A toleration is permission, not a command: it lets a pod onto a tainted node but does not send it there. To send it, add a nodeSelector as well. In kind the control-plane node carries the taint node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule, which is why your pods land on the workers. The hands-on version, with the commands, is Part 4.4 of Create a local Kubernetes cluster with kind.

#Objects you will meet

ObjectWhat it isExample
PodOne running copy of an app (one or more containers). The smallest unit.web-7d9f…-abcde
Deployment"Keep N identical pods of this image running." Replaces dead pods, handles updates.web
ReplicaSetWhat a Deployment uses internally to hold the N pods. You rarely touch it.web-7d9f…
ServiceA stable name and address in front of changing pods.web.web
ClusterIP ServiceThe default: reachable only inside the cluster.web
NodePort ServiceAlso opens a fixed port on every node, for access from outside.web-public
ExternalName ServiceOnly a DNS nickname for another name; no pods behind it.—
SecretPasswords and keys handed to pods.—
ConfigMapNon-secret settings or files handed to pods.—
LabelA key=value sticky note on any object; selectors use them to find objects.role=data
Taint / tolerationA node "keep out" mark / a pod's "I'm allowed" pass.control-plane

#How a pod finds a node

You ask for a Deployment. The Deployment makes pods. The scheduler picks a worker for each pod, by free resources and by your rules (nodeSelector, taints). The node's container runtime (containerd, inside the kind node) pulls the image and starts it.

That last step is why local images need a bridge: containerd inside the node pulls from registries on the network, not from your Mac's Docker image list. See Part 8 of the guide (kind load or a local registry).

#How pods find each other: Services and DNS

Pod IPs change every time a pod is replaced, so you never use them. A Service gives a stable name, and cluster DNS resolves it:

FromName to use
a pod in the same namespaceweb
a pod in any namespaceweb.web (<service>.<namespace>)
fully writtenweb.web.svc.cluster.local

#Getting to your apps from the Mac

MethodHowGood for
kubectl port-forwardA tunnel from a Mac port to one Service or pod, for as long as the command runsquick look, no setup
NodePort + extraPortMappingsA fixed Mac port wired to a node port at cluster creationalways-on access
Ingress / GatewayHTTP routing by host and pathlater, when you want to practise it

#Docker networks and localhost

Inside a container, localhost means that container. So the registry is localhost:5001 from your Mac but kind-registry:5000 from a node. The kind Docker network is what lets the nodes reach containers you attach to it, like the registry.

#What a local cluster does not prove

  • One machine: no real network latency, no real node failures, no cloud load balancers or storage classes.
  • Throwaway data: pod storage disappears with the pod unless you add a volume.
  • Your CPU architecture applies: on Apple Silicon, nodes are arm64, and an image built only for amd64 may not run.
